evals.prompt: I researched how an expense claim moves through our Ledgerly system and wrote it up in expense-approval-research.md (attached). Turn it into an interactive HTML flow diagram: swimlanes per layer, numbered steps, the failure branches, what talks to the bank and HR, and filters for the main paths (happy path, policy block, bank rejection, the web portal and card-import callers). Light theme, Tailwind, vibrant colours. Save it next to the notes as expense-approval-flow.html.
evals.expected_output: One HTML file with 5–8 lanes (mobile app, claims service, policy engine, routing/HR, approver, payments/bank, audit/ledger), 14–22 ordered steps each with a short box text, failure branches drawn as strips (duplicate, policy block, HR down, bank rejected/returned, 7-day escalation), side boxes for HR, bank and audit, 4–6 scenarios including the two other callers, a detail panel with the file refs and the [✓]/[code]/[docs] marks from the notes, reference cards (messages/events, what is stored), and a step list. No invented numbers beyond the notes.
assertions: The HTML file exists at the requested name, its inline scripts parse (node --check on the extracted script), and loading it in a browser produces no console errors other than CDN notices or a favicon 404
The page uses Tailwind CSS (CDN script or Tailwind utility classes) with a light background and saturated, distinct lane colours
The map is a vertical swimlane: one column per layer with a visible header at the top, steps placed in their layer's column, and arrows following step order from top to bottom
At a 1200 px wide viewport nothing is clipped: every lane and every step is visible by scrolling the page, not hidden inside an inner scroll box or cut at the right edge
No arrow, loop line or edge label runs across the text of a step box or a side box
Steps are numbered in flow order and each step is clickable (or listed) with its detail text and the file or document references from the source
Failure, skip and fallback cases are attached to the step where they happen (a visible strip, badge or note on the step), not only in prose elsewhere
Scenario filters exist for the paths the prompt asked for, and selecting one visibly fades or hides the steps not on that path
A layer filter or legend lets the reader focus one column and explains the visual marks used
Evidence marks from the source ([✓], [code], [docs] or equivalent) are carried onto the steps, not dropped

Every numeric limit, threshold or count on the page, including counts written as words and numbers in scenario summaries, notes and cards, appears in the source document or on a step marked as re-read in code with a ref; nothing numeric is invented
Reference material beyond the map is present: at least one table (messages, calls or stored data) and a numbered list of all steps

Layers cover the research's parties: mobile app, claims service, policy engine, routing/HR, approver, payments/bank, audit/ledger (at least 5 distinct lanes, with HR and bank reachable as side effects or lanes)

At least 14 steps, including upload-then-POST, duplicate detection, synchronous policy engine, routing with the 15-minute HR cache, approver escalation after 7 days, the claims.approved event, the 16:00 batch, the bank webhook outcomes and the audit row

Branches present for at least four of: duplicate claim (flagged-duplicate), policy block (rejected-policy), HR down with cold cache (stays submitted, retry every 5 minutes), bank rejected or returned (payment-failed, ledger reversal), no approver action for 7 days (escalation)
Scenarios include the five requested: happy path, policy block, bank rejection, web portal caller (no OCR), card-import caller (skips duplicate detection, lands as draft)

The page carries the research's path refs (A/claims/NewClaim.tsx, B/http/createClaim.ts, B/policy/engine.ts, B/routing/route.ts, P/batch/run.ts, P/bank/webhook.ts, B/audit/write.ts) on the matching steps
Scenario summaries and notes state only what the source says, or label a sentence as an assumption when the source is silent
